Text | Yiying Hao

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

The previous article, Tackling aircraft noise, part 1: its characteristics and the metrics used to model and assess it, described what aircraft noise is like and the harm it does. So can aircraft noise be controlled? And what concrete measures are in place today to reduce its harmful effects?

Internationally, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) sets standards limiting the noise that aircraft emit. In the UK, the Department for Transport (DfT) and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) oversee the environmental aspects of aviation. Under sections 78–80 of the Civil Aviation Act 1982 (as amended in 2006), the Secretary of State has the power to control aircraft noise at designated airports; at present, however, only Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted are designated.

Beyond legislation, national and local governments have issued policies and guidance on managing the noise and vibration impacts of aviation, and current British Standards also cover the assessment of aircraft noise and of other noise and vibration sources associated with airport construction and operation. The key documents include the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF), which guides planning authorities in approving applications, and the Noise Policy Statement for England (NPSE), which sets out the government’s aims on noise, health and quality of life. In October 2017, the government published the revised draft Airports National Policy Statement on airport expansion in the South East of England, the Air Navigation Guidance 2017, and its response to the consultation on UK airspace policy. In addition, CAP1506, the 2014 Survey of Noise Attitudes, was published in February 2017, and CAP1616 on airspace design in December 2017.

The major UK airports also publish noise action plans at regular intervals to limit the impact of aircraft noise on nearby residents, balancing airport growth against environmental protection.

Drawing on current regulations and policies, the noise control measures at major airports and practical project experience, this second article in the series therefore looks at ways of reducing aircraft noise mainly from the perspective of source control. It takes as examples three airports of different sizes: London Heathrow, one of the busiest airports in the world; Manchester Airport, the third busiest in the UK; and the smaller East Midlands Airport. The measures are grouped into aircraft operating procedures, operating restrictions, noise envelopes and other considerations.

1. Aircraft operating procedures

Heathrow, which handles an average of 1,300 flights a day, uses the concept of respite: routes are designed to provide predictable periods of relief, so that noise is not concentrated and continuous, and residents under the flight paths get a break from it.

On departure, for example, aircraft fan out along several Noise Preferential Routes (NPRs) shortly after take-off, spreading the noise burden across several communities. They nevertheless remain concentrated within the NPR “swathes” until they reach 4,000 ft, and only then disperse. Advances in aircraft technology also mean that aircraft now generally reach 4,000 ft much faster than they used to.

On arrival, aircraft become more and more concentrated on the final approach to the runway, all following the same approach path over the last 7.5 nautical miles before landing. For westerly arrivals at Heathrow, this concentration is “spread out” by runway alternation: the landing runway is switched halfway through the day. Making full use of the latest aviation technology also matters, of course; performance-based navigation (PBN), for example, guides aircraft more precisely and efficiently. In addition, continuous descent on arrival and steeper approach angles can effectively reduce the number of residents affected by aircraft noise. Heathrow has set targets for its approach angle of 3.2 degrees by 2030 and 3.5 degrees by 2040.

Source: AirportWatch, April 2012

Manchester Airport operates a system of Preferred Noise Routes (PNRs). In 2012, only 3% of flights left the PNRs (that is, flew “off track”). By 2015, Manchester had run formal trials to establish the benefits that Precision Area Navigation (P-RNAV) departure procedures could bring. Specific measures include the following: all aircraft arriving between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. use a continuous descent procedure; the final approach into Manchester is guided by the Instrument Landing System (ILS), which keeps aircraft on a very narrow descent path at 3°, and aircraft using the ILS must not descend below 2,000 ft before joining the glide path; when approaching from the east, jet aircraft must not join the final approach at a height of less than 1,500 ft; propeller aircraft with a maximum take-off weight above 5,700 kg must not join the final approach less than 3 nautical miles from touchdown or below 1,000 ft; and reverse thrust after landing is avoided, taxiing on engine power is reduced, and non-essential use of auxiliary power units (APUs) is restricted.

Although East Midlands Airport is smaller, it was one of the first airports in Europe to promote continuous descent approaches (CDA), and from 2014 its CDA compliance target was raised to 95%. Departing aircraft must also follow set routes and, where possible, avoid flying over densely populated areas.

2. Aircraft operating restrictions

Heathrow and the Airports Commission agree that operating restrictions should not be the first resort. Heathrow already schedules fewer flights between 23:00 and 06:00 than any other European hub, with a six-and-a-half-hour ban on scheduled night flights. Meanwhile, 90% of its aircraft will be “next-generation” types such as the A380, 787 and A320neo, and “green slots” are given only to airlines willing to operate the quietest aircraft.

To cut aircraft noise drastically, the MIT–Cambridge University silent aircraft design achieves 124 passenger-miles per gallon, nearly 25% better than current aircraft. The Silent Aircraft Initiative was set up to meet the challenge of reducing aircraft noise further as the number of flights keeps growing. Its approach was to make fundamental noise reduction the primary design criterion: to design an aircraft quiet enough to be imperceptible to people in the urban areas around an airport, while remaining competitive with current and next-generation aircraft on fuel burn and emissions. The project’s main result is a conceptual “Silent Aircraft eXperimental.” Compared with today’s civil airliners, its estimated noise level is below the background noise of a densely populated area, and it is expected to use 23% less fuel.

Source: Aero-Astro Magazine Highlight – The Silent Aircraft

Manchester Airport, however, applies further measures to aircraft operations. It encourages greater use of quieter aircraft, closes Runway 2 at certain times and keeps simultaneous use of both runways to a minimum. Daytime flights that exceed a maximum noise level of 90 dB(A) are fined, and engine tests outside the engine test pen are limited in timing and number. Night-time restrictions are stricter still: the number of ordinary night flights is limited, non-standard departures are normally not permitted at night, visual approaches are not allowed between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m., and all landing aircraft must follow continuous descent procedures between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.

Likewise, East Midlands Airport strictly limits night-time operations. Only scheduled aircraft may take off during or after the night period. Older, noisier aircraft may not be scheduled to depart at night, and if such an aircraft is delayed past its scheduled departure time and still takes off, a night noise surcharge is paid into the airport’s community fund.

3. Noise envelopes

The previous article in this series mentioned the noise envelope. One of its key elements is limiting the inputs, namely the number of flights and the flight paths. A large airport such as Heathrow focuses mainly on the number of flights and caps take-offs and landings: under the planning agreement for Heathrow Terminal 5, air transport movements (ATMs) are limited to 480,000 a year. Heathrow currently operates close to that limit, but thanks to improvements in technology its Leq noise contours are shrinking. As the various noise reduction measures are strengthened, Heathrow’s Lden 55 dB noise contour is expected to cover an ever smaller area.

Manchester Airport’s requirements focus more on flight paths and timing: non-standard departures are limited to no more than 5% a year, and departure track deviations are capped at 5% a year. Any airline that persistently fails to keep to the Preferred Noise Routes (PNRs) must pay a surcharge, and flights scheduled to take off or land at night must not exceed 7% of all flights. East Midlands Airport has also set up a long-term noise envelope that tightly controls night flights, giving local communities stronger guarantees on noise control.

4. Other considerations

Beyond the measures above, the airport’s land and geography should also be taken into account: for instance, whether more routes should be laid over uninhabited areas such as lakes and the sea. Sydney Airport is a good example. In addition, a range of measures, including land-use planning around the airport, relocation assistance schemes, property purchase, sound insulation grant schemes, sound insulation of noise-sensitive buildings within the noise contours, and community trust funds, all directly reduce the harm done by aircraft noise. In the next article in this series, I will look at these measures for protecting noise receivers in more detail.

So, with guidance from policy and regulation, effective control measures at airports and better aircraft technology, the noise impact around airports can fall rather than rise. Airports need not keep getting louder.

About the author: Yiying Hao (PhD in architecture and former postdoctoral researcher, University of Sheffield) is a senior engineer at Bureau Veritas in Manchester. Research interests: acoustic environment assessment for major infrastructure, large-scale noise mapping, and soundscape design and assessment. Yiying has led or played a major role in research and implementation projects on aircraft noise assessment, policy revision and soundscape design for several international airports, including Heathrow, Manchester, Dublin and Manston.
